question: Let \(N\) be the positive integer \(7777\ldots777,\) a \(313\)-digit number where each digit is a \(7.\) Let \(f(r)\) be the leading digit of the \(r\)th root of \(N.\) What is \[ \begin{aligned} &f(2)+f(3)+f(4)\\ &\quad{}+f(5)+f(6)? \end{aligned} \]
solution:
Multiplying a positive number by a power of \(10\) only moves its decimal point, so it preserves the leading digit. We can use this to reduce each enormous root to a small number that can be bounded exactly.

Because \(N\) has \(313\) digits and begins with \(7\),
\[
7\cdot10^{312}<N<8\cdot10^{312}.
\]
Write \(N=a\cdot10^{312}\), where \(7<a<8\).

The exponent \(312\) is divisible by \(2,3,4,6\). For these root indices,
\[
\sqrt[r]{N}=\sqrt[r]{a}\cdot10^{312/r}.
\]
The power of ten does not affect the leading digit, so we only need \(\sqrt[r]{a}\).

Since \(2^2=4<a<9=3^2\), we have \(2<\sqrt a<3\), giving \(f(2)=2\).

For \(r=3,4,6\), the number \(a\) lies strictly between \(1^r\) and \(2^r\): the upper powers are \(8,16,64\), respectively. Thus each of these roots lies between \(1\) and \(2\), giving
\[
f(3)=f(4)=f(6)=1.
\]

The fifth root needs a different decimal shift because \(312=5\cdot62+2\). In this case,
\[
\sqrt[5]{N}=10^{62}\sqrt[5]{100a}.
\]
Now
\[
3^5=243<700<100a<800<1024=4^5.
\]
Therefore \(3<\sqrt[5]{100a}<4\), so \(f(5)=3\).

The requested sum is
\[
2+1+1+3+1=\boxed{8},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
